title: Silent Keyboards and LLMs: Going Through the Motions
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood uses the story of Rachmaninoff practising on a silent keyboard aboard a ship to America in 1909 as an extended metaphor for how writers and students use large language models. The silent keyboard was useful to Rachmaninoff because he already had a trained inner ear, a capacity for revision and a concrete performance to prepare for, whereas an LLM offers no such guarantee that its output corresponds to real thinking. Underwood argues that an LLM brings every request to the same level of fluent, plausible prose and that regeneration can substitute for the repetition that actually changes a writer's mind. He then shows that classrooms are already full of silent keyboards, from keyword shortcuts in maths to cookbook labs and the five-paragraph essay, which let students go through the motions without the real disciplinary practice. His closing worry is that novices lack the ear, discipline and purpose to benefit, so they get the clicks without the music.
points: The silent keyboard helped Rachmaninoff because he already had an inner ear, openness to revision and a real performance as the purpose of practice.
An LLM brings every request to the same keybed of fluent prose, so it cannot signal whether the thinking behind a sentence is the writer's own.
Writers who keep their attention on choosing, revising and rejecting their own sentences control the tool, while careless prompting makes the human look foolish.
Many classroom routines, such as keyword shortcuts, cookbook labs and the five-paragraph essay, already work as silent keyboards that reward completion over thinking.
For novices, silent practice becomes the curriculum itself, which makes LLMs a risk to students who lack ear, discipline and purpose.
quotes: The reason an LLM is a lot like a silent keyboard has nothing to do with noise. It has to do with going through the motions divorced from participation in social, cultural, and historical reality.
Offering an LLM’s output as one's own writing is like walking onstage, playing the audience a recording of clicks, and calling it the Third Concerto.
An LLM brings every request to the same keybed level of fluent, plausible prose, however shallow or profound the thought that prompted it or that arrived in the output was.
Repetition on the silent board becomes regeneration in the LLM. At sea, Rachmaninoff repeated his own stroke until his fingers changed.
Classrooms are full of devices that function as silent keyboards. They have their place on a passenger ship and need to be reckoned with in anyone’s model of learning in crowded quarters.

Most classroom feedback, Hattie and Timperley (2007) found, tells students whether a task was done correctly, not how the thinking behind it went. For an expert, silent keyboards can train the hand. For a novice, the silence becomes the curriculum.
Discipline gave him the ear; experiment gave him the freedom to use it.
School work is usually valuable once it is over and done, graded, and forgotten. That’s a problem with LLMs on every screen. Too many silent keyboards, too few concerts.
